blocks.text: Solomon adds that the semamith is in kings' palaces. This was the one objection that Mercerus had to raise [col. 1090]. "Our translator," he says, "renders semamith as stellio, which does not seem to fit, because it does not live in the courts of kings." But that the stellio lives in houses was not, I believe, unknown to this most learned man, since nearly all who have written about the stellio proclaim it with one voice. Thus in Eusebius, Porphyry speaks of κατοικιδίους σκαλαβώτας [katoikidious skalabōtas], domestic stellios. Suidas, the Etymologicum, Phavorinus and others among the Greeks define it as ζωΰφιον ἐοικὸς σαύρᾳ ἐν τοῖς τοίχοις τῶν οἰκημάτων ἀνέρπον [zōyphion eoikos saura en tois toichois tōn oikēmatōn anerpon], a little animal like a lizard, creeping along the walls of houses. So also Elluchasem, a physician of Baghdad, in his book On Animals: The stellio is a lizard that inhabits houses. Hence Kiranides calls it τοιχοβάτην [toichobatēn]. And in Spain the Catalans call it dragon de las casas, that is, dragon of the houses. That it lives especially in old buildings is reported by Niphus on Aristotle and by Ponzettus in his book On Poisons. But that it is also seen in new ones is asserted by Marcellinus in Hermolaus. According to the Philosopher ^{f)} it lives in mangers; according to Antoninus Liberalis ^{g)}, παρ᾽ ὀχετὸν [par᾽ ocheton], near drains; according to Pliny ^{h)}, about doors and windows, or in caves or tombs; according to Arnobius ^{i)}, it builds its nests under the hollows of statues. Matthiolus ^{k)} assigns to it the hollows of walls near the ground. But the ancients assign it ceiling panels and the vaults of roofs, where it may walk upside down. Accordingly, besides Aristophanes and Dioscorides, whom I have already cited above ^{l)}, you may also read in Avicenna ^{m)} that the stellio sometimes falls from above into a drink and turns it [II, 520] into poison if it dies in it ^{(4)}. These things, if I am not mistaken, amply prove that the stellio is not a wild animal but a domestic one. Further, I see no privilege by which royal houses should be immune from this pest. Indeed, the greater the pile and mass of stones in them, the deeper are the fissures and cracks in the walls. From this you may not unreasonably conclude that such little animals, which live mostly in holes in walls, dwell even more safely in the courts and palaces of kings than in a private house.
